pages.title: Motivation today
claims: What is the best practices for scaling and hparam tuning LMs?
Does chinchilla’s approach to scaling actually work?
Can we save compute when training and fitting these things?
Should we be picking particular architectures / parametrizations to scale nicely?

pages.title: Scaling in practice
claims: The newest model we talked about with scaling details - 2022
What about more recently?

pages.title: Initialization and optimizers
claims: Initialization, optimizers, and various hyperparams (LR/batch) can be scale sensitive

pages.title: Working through some detailed, public scaling recipes
claims: 1. MiniCPM
2. DeepSeek

pages.title: MiniCPM
claims: MiniCPM (2024) – small, high-perf LM from Tsinghua group.
Careful, extensive scaling computations + muP to stabilize and simplify scaling
Not really ‘sota’ model (even in 2024) but many interesting lessons on scaling

pages.title: MiniCPM
claims: High performance 1-2.5 B parameter models. These models beat most out 2Bs and
match many modern 7B models.

pages.title: Techique 1: muP to stabilize scaling
claims: Scale_emb = 12, scale_depth = 1.4, init_std = 0.1, lr =0.01

pages.title: Scaling recipe / strategy
claims: Use muP for initialization, fix the aspect ratio, scale up the overall model size.
Note that the gap between the largest model here and the actual model they train is ~5x
Optimal batch, LR, token-to-size ratios are directly fitted via scaling analysis

pages.title: Optimal LR
claims: According to muP – optimal learning rate should be (roughly) stable. Is it?

pages.title: Optimal batch
claims: Three model sizes (9m, 30m, 170m) as a function of data size (y), batch (x) and loss (col)
Vertical columns of points represent a single training curve (fixed batch, more points).
Red line attempts to identify minimum loss points for each y-value
– this is the ‘optimal batch size’ for a model size / dataset size combination.

pages.title: Optimal batch size
claims: We can then follow the Kaplan 2020 analysis and plot optimal batch size vs final loss.
Fairly clean trend – polynomially increase the batch size as loss decreases.

pages.title: What remains – model size vs data tradeoffs.
claims: From chinchilla – to fit a scaling law, we need to train from scratch, not just early stop
This turns the cost of fitting a scaling law from n to n^2.. Can we avoid this?

pages.title: (partial) solution in miniCPM – WSD learning rate
claims: Instead of cosine, split learning rate into warmup, stable, and decay phases.
For chinchilla-style analysis, can restart the run at the end of the stable phase.

pages.title: WSD learning rates work well in miniCPM
claims: Slower during the stable phase, rapid loss decay during decay phase. Decay ~ 10%.

pages.title: Chinchilla-type analysis
claims: Equipped with the WSD learning rate,
we can now try to find the optimal data-to-model size ratio
MiniCPM authors choose method 1 (lower envelope) and method 3 (joint fit)

pages.title: Chinchlla method 1
claims: Fairly clear (though maybe not linear?) trends
Different colors indicate different models. Their runs suggest relatively low diminishing
returns due to data.

pages.title: Chinchilla method 3
claims: Their primary scaling approach is the joint fit – they find very high data-model ratios.

pages.title: DeepSeek
claims: DeepSeek (2024) – another LM with careful scaling analysis
7 and 67B param models – generally high performance compared to other open LM

pages.title: Scaling strategy – batch + LR
claims: Scaling strategy: don’t use any muP, directly estimate optimal batch / LR

pages.title: Scaling analysis of learning rates
claims: Small scale runs + collect ‘near optimal’ (within 0.25% of min) models.
Learning rate fit looks a bit questionable..

pages.title: For chinchilla analysis: WSD-style learning rate
claims: Deepseek uses WSD-style learning rate – fast warmup + two decay steps of 10% each.
Generally seems to match performance of cosine learning rates.

pages.title: Data-size tradeoff analysis: Chinchilla method 2
claims: Straightforward isoflop-style analysis for selecting the model size tradeoffs.

pages.title: Scaling predicts final model loss
claims: The fitted scaling models (generally) accurately predict the final model losses.

pages.title: Hunyuan (2024) large scaling laws

Optimal ratio – 96-1 (data to active param)

pages.title: LLaMA 3 (2024) Scaling laws

pages.title: Recent scaling law recipes

Assume most transformer hypers are invariant to scale
Use a piecewise-linear schedule to make chinchilla scaling cheap.

pages.title: Core question – scaling rates on LR and batch
claims: What are the right variables / functional form?
Different views:
Critical batch: batch as a function of loss (OpenAI)
Compute power law: poly function of compute (DeepSeek)

pages.title: What is muP robust to?
claims: Modern LMs have many components that deviate from muP’s theory
Activations – SwiGLU and squared relu
Batch sizes – Large / small
Initialization variations – zero attention, etc.
RMS norm gains
Exotic optimizers (Lion)
Regularizers
Which of these (if any) break muP?

pages.title: What is muP not robust to? RMSnorm gain
claims: In our arch – RMSNorm has learnable gains. This turns out to break muP
But these gains can be removed with little loss of perf..

pages.title: What is muP not robust to? Exotic optimizers
claims: There are other, exotic optimizers based on just gradient signs. Do they transfer?

pages.title: What is muP not robust to? – (strong) weight decay
claims: What about strong (0.1) weight decay? – this is maybe the only significant muP failure

pages.title: Is muP useful? At least to some extent..
claims: Overall, muP generally seems useful – insofar that SP is quite a bit more unstable.
Current evidence suggests that muP parametrization / initialization may be easier to tune.

pages.title: Recap: scaling in the wild
claims: What are challenges in scaling ‘in practice’
1. Setting model arch hyperparameters ( width, etc)
2. Setting optimizer hyperparameters (LR, batch)
3. Compute needed to fit the big chinchilla sweep
Some solutions?
1. Assume stability (or use muP)
2. Search for optimal LR / batch in small scale, either keep fixed or predict scaling
3. Use alternative learning schedules (WSD-like)
